ACLED

In a previous class, we talked about using sources like V-DEM to get country-level measures of things like state repression, democratic institutions, and other aspects of the political opportunity structure. In this class, we’ll explore a data source that measures state repression at the event level rather than the country-year level.

Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) is a project that records both violent and non-violent conflict events and “strategic developments” around the world. The project initially collected data on Africa and the Middle east, but, since 2021, they have expanded their scope to include the entire globe.

They update their data every two weeks, however, their most accessible data sets are now released with a one year lag.

Installing a couple packages

Install the packages below by removing the # and executing each line of code.

# install.packages("usethis")
# install.packages("acledR")
# install.packages('zoo')

Signing up for an ACLED account

Head over to the ACLED website and follow the instructions to register an account. For now, copy-paste your password and email address into a text file so you can use it later. Be sure to use your .umd email address and select “academic” as your affiliation to ensure you get the highest level of free access.

Storing your login info

We’ll be using the acledR package to interact with the data from within R. To use the commands from this package, you’ll need to send your password and email address as arguments. You could do this by just copying those values directly into a script, but that’s a bad way to store private information.

To get around this problem, we’ll assign the password and email addresses as environment variables that we can access in R using the function Sys.getenv

To set this up, run this line to open the .Renviron file in a new window in R-studio:

usethis::edit_r_environ()

You’ll want to create two new lines in this file: one with the email address you used to register, and another with your ACLED password. The password and email address should both be enclosed in quotation marks. Here’s an example of how that might look:

When you’re finished, be sure you save the changes to your your .Renviron file. Then, you’ll need to restart R-studio. If you’ve set this up correctly, running Sys.getenv('acled_email') in your console should return the email address you just used to sign up.

Sys.getenv('acled_email')
[1] "nlund@umd.edu"

Sending a query

Now that we’ve got our password and username set up as environment variables, we can send a query using the acledR package.

The code below will return data on events in China since 2018. The population argument will also return an estimate of the population that was “exposed” to each event.

Note that I could also filter events by event_type, country, or inter_code (numeric interaction code):

library(acledR)
library(tidyverse)

result<-acled_api(
  email = Sys.getenv('acled_email'),
  password = Sys.getenv('acled_password'),
  population ='best',
  start_date = '2018-01-01',
  end_date = '2024-12-31',
  country = 'China')



result|>
  mutate(counter_demonstrators = str_detect(tags, "counter-demonstration"))|>
  filter(counter_demonstrators == TRUE)
TipBackup

If you’re not able to get this working yet, you can download a copy of this data by running this code:

result<-read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Neilblund/GVPT429KFall2026/refs/heads/master/Data/acled_china_2018_2024.csv')

If you’re planning to use data from ACLED for an analysis, I would recommend saving your results so you can avoid the need to send the same query over and over:

write_csv(result, file='acled_china_2018_2024.csv')

Now that you have a saved file, you can read data back into R with the read_csv function:

result<-read_csv('acled_china_2018_2024.csv')

Using the data

ACLED codes up to 31 different characteristics of each event. You can read additional details about these event characteristics on their website. The list is quite expansive, and we’ll often need to use these variables to filter data to identify the information we’re interested in for an analysis.

Event types, interaction types, and geography

Where possible, ACLED records the locations of each event. Sometimes this isn’t very specific: some sources may only report a country or administrative region for a protest, but in other cases, news reports will indicate a specific city or even a specific street when discussing an event. You can get a sense for the level of specificity for a location by looking at the geo_precision column for an event:

table(result$geo_precision)

   1    2    3 
8909 5158 1371

I’m going to use the admin1 variable, which records the general administrative region for each event, to identify events that took place in Hong Kong only. I’ll just use filter to get a set of events:

hk<-result|>
  filter(admin1 == "Hong Kong")

Note that there is a complex typology of event types represented here. You can read more about the event typology here. The most unusual class of events are “Strategic developments”. These includes things like states gaining or losing territory, or declarations of states of emergency, or targeted assassinations. ACLED includes some addition detail on how these work on their website, but for our purposes, we’re just going to put them in a separate data set entirely.

strategic_developments<-hk|>
  filter(event_type == "Strategic developments")

hk_events<-hk|>
    filter(event_type !='Strategic developments')

Finally, I’ll use counts of the interactions column to get counts of the groups that interacted with each other in Hong Kong:

interaction<-hk_events|>
  count(interaction)


ggplot(interaction, aes(x=reorder(interaction, n), y=n)) + 
  geom_bar(stat='identity')  +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(y='Number of events',
       x ='Interaction type'
       )

On your own

Use the sub_event_type column to get a bar graph with counts of the following types of activity: violent demonstrations, excessive force against protesters, protest with intervention, and peaceful protests.

Searching for a specific type of event

In many cases, we’ll want to filter results to include a specific type of event. For instance, I might be interested in identifying protests related to the corona virus outbreak. Although ACLED doesn’t explicitly categorize protests this way, they do include a “notes” column that has a brief summary of each event.

In many cases, I can filter data based on the contents of the notes column. However, because this is free text, I can’t just do something like filter(notes == "covid"), instead, I’ll use a regular expression, which is a language that can be used to match specific patterns in text.

Regular expressions are extremely flexible, and we can use them to identify some really complex patterns. In this case, however, we can use a relatively simple RegEx to capture our data: we basically just want events where the notes column contains words like “coronavirus” or “covid-19”.

The str_detect function will take a column and a regular expression and will return TRUE for any elements of the column where there is a matching pattern:

string = c("A sentence containing covid",
           "A sentence that shouldn't be matched"
           )

str_detect(string, "covid")
[1]  TRUE FALSE

So, we can use str_detect to extract rows where the notes column contains the string “covid”:

result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "covid"))|>
  nrow()
[1] 0

This doesn’t return any data, however because our expression is case-sensitive. If I wanted to capture instances where covid occurred in lower case OR upper case, I could use a slightly modified version of this expression. Using the square brackets [], I can define a “character set” where the expression will evaluate to TRUE if any single character in the set is match. So the code below matches EITHER “Covid” or “covid”:

result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "[cC]ovid"))|>
  nrow()
[1] 17

This is still too low! That sort of makes sense, because there’s more than one name for Covid 19. I can extend my regular expression further by using the pipe operator (“|”) which works like a logical OR operator. So the code below will match EITHER covid, Covid, corona, or Corona:

result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "[cC]ovid|[Cc]orona"))|>
  nrow()
[1] 689

That gets us a far more plausible result.

c19<-result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "[cC]ovid|[Cc]orona"))

Making an event timeline

We’ll use our results to create a timeline of Covid-related protests and riots in China between 2018 through 2024.

To do this, we’ll start by using the familiar filter and count functions to create a data frame with a number of protests or riots per day:

events_count<-c19|>
  filter(event_type%in% c("Protests", "Riots"))|>
  count(event_date,event_type)

Next, we’ll need to use the complete function to fill in zeros for days where no event occurred.

events_count<-events_count|>
  complete(event_date = full_seq(event_date, period=1), # get a complete sequence of days
           nesting(event_type),                         # nest by the grouping variable
           fill=list(n=0)                               # fill empty rows with 0
           )

Finally, we’ll group by event_type and create a rolling 30-day count of each event type using the rollsum function from the zoo package.

events_count<-events_count|>
  group_by(event_type)|>
  mutate(rolling_count = zoo::rollsum(n, 
                                      k=30,  # the size of the rolling window
                                      na.pad=T,
                                      align='right'
                                      ))

The result of this set of functions is a dataframe with a rolling count of protest events related to Covid. Now we can use this to create a line plot that will show the temporal patterns in protest activity over time:

event_timeline<-ggplot(events_count,aes(x=event_date, y=rolling_count,  color = event_type))  + 
  geom_line() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x='date', 
       y='30 day rolling count of events',
       color = 'event type',
       title ='Covid related protests in China',
       caption ='Source: ACLED'
       ) +
  # this will give us a tick mark every 4 months:
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b '%y", 
               date_breaks = '3 month'
               )


event_timeline

The results here should raise some immediate questions in your mind. For instance: it might prompt you to ask what factors explain the ebb and flow of activity over the course of the pandemic, and you might take a look at the “Strategic developments” or read some news coverage to try to get a better sense of when and why the activity levels shifted.

In some cases, it might make sense to include a short annotation to mark significant events that happened at different points during the timeframe of interest. The code below adds a text annotation that marks when the Chinese government began to abandon their highly restrictive “zero Covid” policies:

event_timeline + 
  annotate(geom='label', 
           x =as.Date('2022-12-07'), 
           y=61, 
           label='December 7, 2022: gov. loosens Covid restrictions')

On your own

Follow the steps you used above to get a timeline of protest activity in Hong Kong over this same time frame.

Repression

Each ACLED event includes one or more additional “tags” that simplify identifying and filtering certain kinds of events. Some of these tags apply to only specific regions or time periods, and a single event may contain more than one tag. You can read more here.

In 2025, ACLED began including additional “conflict category” tags on all events since 2020. These include Repression, Insurgency, Atrocities,Terrorist activity and Foreign military engagement. We’ll try using the “Repression” tag to get a sense of what countries were using the most repression in some data from last year.

Note that we’re pulling data for all countries, so we’re going to pull data for a smaller time frame to ensure we can get a manageable amount of data. We’ll also use the event_types option to remove all “Strategic developments”, since these will never be tagged as repression events.

global_result<-acled_api(
  email = Sys.getenv('acled_email'),
  password = Sys.getenv('acled_password'),
  start_date = Sys.Date()-393,  # last year minus 4 more weeks
  end_date =Sys.Date()-365,     # last year
  population ='best',
  event_types = c('Battles', 
                  'Violence against civilians', 
                  'Protests', 
                  'Riots',
                  'Explosions/Remote violence'
                  )
  )

# saving the results to a file so we don't need to pull this again
write_csv(global_result, file='acled_global_events_October_2025.csv')
TipBackup

If you’re not able to get this working yet, you can download a copy of this data by running this code:

global_result<-read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Neilblund/GVPT429KFall2026/refs/heads/master/Data/acled_global_events_October_2025.csv')

Once we have our data, we’ll do some additional filtering to identify repression events:

repression<-global_result|>
  filter(str_detect(tags, "Repression"))

From here, we might do something like: aggregate the data to identify which countries had the highest number of repression related events during the time frame covered:

repression|>
  group_by(country)|>
  summarize( n = n() )|> # getting the number of obs in each group
  arrange(-n)|>          # sorting in reverse order of frequency
  slice_head(n=10)       # getting the top 10

We could also visualize this using something like a bar plot:

repression|>
  group_by(country)|>
  summarize( n = n() )|> 
  arrange(-n)|>          
  slice_head(n=10)|>
  ggplot(aes(y=reorder(country, n), # sorting the labels by n
             x=n)) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x= "Number of repression events",
       y = "Country",
       title ="Top 10 countries by number of repression events (October 2025)",
       caption = "Source: ACLED"
       )

On your own

Modify the code above to create a bar plot showing the top 10 countries in order of the total number of fatalities in repression related events.

Interactive event mapping

We can use the leaflet package to create an interactive map of protest events in Hong Kong. Note that this kind of interactive plot only works with HTML formatted output, so you would need to use Rmarkdown to knit this as html before you could share it with someone else. That said, this can be a useful way to get a better grasp of your data even if you don’t end up sharing it with anyone else.

# install.packages("osmdata")
# install.packages("leaflet")
# install.packages('glue')

Start by creating a base mapping layer using the addProviderTiles function. This will just create an empty world map. You can try zooming in to look at specific areas here:

library(leaflet)

base_map <- leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldStreetMap")  
base_map

We’ll use the getbb function from the osmdata package to get the coordinates for Hong Kong. This will make it so our base map is automatically zoomed in to show the area of interest:

hkbox  <- osmdata::getbb("Hong Kong, China")

event_map <- base_map |>
  fitBounds(
    lng1 = hkbox[1],
    lng2 = hkbox[3],
    lat1 = hkbox[2],
    lat2 = hkbox[4]
  )

event_map

Finally, we’ll make some formatted pop-up markers that will show a bit more information about each event. The glue function here performs string interpolation, and the <br> tags are just HTML that creates a line break (this will be easier to understand once you take a look at the map)

For the sake of keeping things manageable, we’ll only look at events that happened in 2019. I’ll also remove events with low levels of geographic precision.

hk_map_events <- hk_events|>
  filter(year(event_date) == 2019)|>
  filter(geo_precision == 1)|> # removing low-precision events
  mutate(formatted_notes = glue::glue('Date: {event_date}
                                      <br>
                                      Actor 1: {actor1}
                                      <br>
                                      Actor 2: {actor2}
                                      <br>
                                      Action: {sub_event_type}
                                      <br>
                                      Description: {notes}
                                      '))

Now we’ll add markers for each event. Since many events happened in the same location, we’ll use the markerClusterOPtions function to create a clustered marker that will spread out when we click or zoom in on a location:

clustered_map <- event_map |>
  addAwesomeMarkers(
    data = hk_map_events,
    lng =  ~ longitude,
    lat =  ~ latitude,
    #icon = makeAwesomeIcon(icon = "Home", library = "glyphicon",
    #                       markerColor = 'red'
    #                       ), # uncomment to change the marker style 
    
    # groups together overlapping markers. Zoom in to show events
    clusterOptions = markerClusterOptions(),
    
    # create a popup to show additional info on reported events on click
    popup =  ~ formatted_notes
    
  )



clustered_map

You can also try swapping out the default basemap for something less “busy” using the addProviderTiles() function. (Note that using some of these may require you to sign up for an account)

clustered_map|>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.NatGeoWorldMap")

In a previous class, we talked about using sources like V-DEM to get country-level measures of things like state repression, democratic institutions, and other aspects of the political opportunity structure. In this class, we'll explore a data source that measures state repression at the event level rather than the country-year level.

Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) is a project that records both violent and non-violent conflict events and "strategic developments" around the world. The project initially collected data on Africa and the Middle east, but, since 2021, they have expanded their scope to include the entire globe.

They update their data every two weeks, however, their most accessible data sets are now released with a one year lag.

## Installing a couple packages

Install the packages below by removing the `#` and executing each line of code.

```{r}
# install.packages("usethis")
# install.packages("acledR")
# install.packages('zoo')
```

## Signing up for an ACLED account

Head over to [the ACLED website](https://acleddata.com/user/register) and follow the instructions to register an account. For now, copy-paste your password and email address into a text file so you can use it later. Be sure to use your `.umd` email address and select "academic" as your affiliation to ensure you get the highest level of free access.

## Storing your login info

We'll be using the `acledR` package to interact with the data from within R. To use the commands from this package, you'll need to send your password and email address as arguments. You *could* do this by just copying those values directly into a script, but that's a bad way to store private information.

To get around this problem, we'll assign the password and email addresses as environment variables that we can access in R using the function `Sys.getenv`

To set this up, run this line to open the `.Renviron` file in a new window in R-studio:

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}

usethis::edit_r_environ()

```

You'll want to create two new lines in this file: one with the email address you used to register, and another with your ACLED password. The password and email address should both be enclosed in quotation marks. Here's an example of how that might look:

![](../images/renviron_edits.png)

When you're finished, be sure you **save the changes to your your `.Renviron` file**. Then, you'll need to restart R-studio. If you've set this up correctly, running `Sys.getenv('acled_email')` in your console should return the email address you just used to sign up.

```{r}
Sys.getenv('acled_email')

```

## Sending a query

Now that we've got our password and username set up as environment variables, we can send a query using the [`acledR`](https://dtacled.github.io/acledR/) package.

The code below will return data on events in China since 2018. The `population` argument will also return an estimate of the population that was "exposed" to each event.

Note that I could also filter events by `event_type`, `country`, or `inter_code` (numeric interaction code):

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}

library(acledR)
library(tidyverse)

result<-acled_api(
  email = Sys.getenv('acled_email'),
  password = Sys.getenv('acled_password'),
  population ='best',
  start_date = '2018-01-01',
  end_date = '2024-12-31',
  country = 'China')



result|>
  mutate(counter_demonstrators = str_detect(tags, "counter-demonstration"))|>
  filter(counter_demonstrators == TRUE)


```


::: {.callout-tip title="Backup"}

If you're not able to get this working yet, you can download a copy of this data by running this code:

```{r}
result<-read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Neilblund/GVPT429KFall2026/refs/heads/master/Data/acled_china_2018_2024.csv')


```

:::



If you're planning to use data from ACLED for an analysis, I would recommend saving your results so you can avoid the need to send the same query over and over:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
write_csv(result, file='acled_china_2018_2024.csv')

```

Now that you have a saved file, you can read data back into R with the `read_csv` function:

```{r}
result<-read_csv('acled_china_2018_2024.csv')

```

## Using the data

ACLED codes up to 31 different characteristics of each event. You can read additional details about these event characteristics on [their website](https://acleddata.com/methodology/acled-codebook). The list is quite expansive, and we'll often need to use these variables to filter data to identify the information we're interested in for an analysis.

### Event types, interaction types, and geography

Where possible, ACLED records the locations of each event. Sometimes this isn't very specific: some sources may only report a country or administrative region for a protest, but in other cases, news reports will indicate a specific city or even a specific street when discussing an event. You can get a sense for the level of specificity for a location by looking at the `geo_precision` column for an event:

```{r}
table(result$geo_precision)


```

I'm going to use the `admin1` variable, which records the general administrative region for each event, to identify events that took place in Hong Kong only. I'll just use `filter` to get a set of events:

```{r}
hk<-result|>
  filter(admin1 == "Hong Kong")

```

Note that there is a complex typology of event types represented here. You can read more about the event typology [here](https://acleddata.com/methodology/acled-codebook#acled-events-2). The most unusual class of events are "Strategic developments". These includes things like states gaining or losing territory, or declarations of states of emergency, or targeted assassinations. ACLED includes some addition detail on how these work [on their website](https://acleddata.com/methodology/strategic-developments-acled-dataset), but for our purposes, we're just going to put them in a separate data set entirely.

```{r}
strategic_developments<-hk|>
  filter(event_type == "Strategic developments")

hk_events<-hk|>
    filter(event_type !='Strategic developments')


```

Finally, I'll use counts of the `interactions` column to get counts of the groups that interacted with each other in Hong Kong:

```{r}
interaction<-hk_events|>
  count(interaction)


ggplot(interaction, aes(x=reorder(interaction, n), y=n)) + 
  geom_bar(stat='identity')  +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(y='Number of events',
       x ='Interaction type'
       )


```

### Searching for a specific type of event

In many cases, we'll want to filter results to include a specific type of event. For instance, I might be interested in identifying protests related to the corona virus outbreak. Although ACLED doesn't explicitly categorize protests this way, they do include a "notes" column that has a brief summary of each event.

In many cases, I can filter data based on the contents of the notes column. However, because this is free text, I can't just do something like `filter(notes == "covid")`, instead, I'll use a [regular expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression), which is a language that can be used to match specific patterns in text.

Regular expressions are extremely flexible, and we can use them to identify some really complex patterns. In this case, however, we can use a relatively simple RegEx to capture our data: we basically just want events where the notes column contains words like "coronavirus" or "covid-19".

The [`str_detect`](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/reference/str_detect.html) function will take a column and a regular expression and will return `TRUE` for any elements of the column where there is a matching pattern:

```{r}
string = c("A sentence containing covid",
           "A sentence that shouldn't be matched"
           )

str_detect(string, "covid")

```

So, we can use `str_detect` to extract rows where the `notes` column contains the string "covid":

```{r}
result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "covid"))|>
  nrow()




```

This doesn't return any data, however because our expression is case-sensitive. If I wanted to capture instances where covid occurred in lower case OR upper case, I could use a slightly modified version of this expression. Using the square brackets `[]`, I can define a "character set" where the expression will evaluate to TRUE if any single character in the set is match. So the code below matches EITHER "Covid" or "covid":

```{r}
result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "[cC]ovid"))|>
  nrow()


```

This is still too low! That sort of makes sense, because there's more than one name for Covid 19. I can extend my regular expression further by using the pipe operator ("`|`") which works like a logical OR operator. So the code below will match EITHER covid, Covid, corona, or Corona:

```{r}
result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "[cC]ovid|[Cc]orona"))|>
  nrow()

```

That gets us a far more plausible result.

```{r}
c19<-result|>
  filter(str_detect(notes,  "[cC]ovid|[Cc]orona"))



```

### Making an event timeline

We'll use our results to create a timeline of Covid-related protests and riots in China between 2018 through 2024.

To do this, we'll start by using the familiar `filter` and `count` functions to create a data frame with a number of protests or riots per day:

```{r}
events_count<-c19|>
  filter(event_type%in% c("Protests", "Riots"))|>
  count(event_date,event_type)

```

Next, we'll need to use the `complete` function to fill in zeros for days where no event occurred.

```{r}
events_count<-events_count|>
  complete(event_date = full_seq(event_date, period=1), # get a complete sequence of days
           nesting(event_type),                         # nest by the grouping variable
           fill=list(n=0)                               # fill empty rows with 0
           )

```

Finally, we'll group by event_type and create a rolling 30-day count of each event type using the `rollsum` function from the `zoo` package.

```{r}
events_count<-events_count|>
  group_by(event_type)|>
  mutate(rolling_count = zoo::rollsum(n, 
                                      k=30,  # the size of the rolling window
                                      na.pad=T,
                                      align='right'
                                      )) 
  


```

The result of this set of functions is a dataframe with a rolling count of protest events related to Covid. Now we can use this to create a line plot that will show the temporal patterns in protest activity over time:

```{r, fig.width=12}
event_timeline<-ggplot(events_count,aes(x=event_date, y=rolling_count,  color = event_type))  + 
  geom_line() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x='date', 
       y='30 day rolling count of events',
       color = 'event type',
       title ='Covid related protests in China',
       caption ='Source: ACLED'
       ) +
  # this will give us a tick mark every 4 months:
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b '%y", 
               date_breaks = '3 month'
               )


event_timeline



```

The results here should raise some immediate questions in your mind. For instance: it might prompt you to ask what factors explain the ebb and flow of activity over the course of the pandemic, and you might take a look at the "Strategic developments" or read some news coverage to try to get a better sense of when and why the activity levels shifted.

In some cases, it might make sense to include a short annotation to mark significant events that happened at different points during the timeframe of interest. The code below adds a text annotation that marks when the Chinese government began to abandon their highly restrictive "zero Covid" policies:

```{r, fig.width=12}

event_timeline + 
  annotate(geom='label', 
           x =as.Date('2022-12-07'), 
           y=61, 
           label='December 7, 2022: gov. loosens Covid restrictions')


```

## Repression

Each ACLED event includes one or more additional "tags" that simplify identifying and filtering certain kinds of events. Some of these tags apply to only specific regions or time periods, and a single event may contain more than one tag. [You can read more here](https://acleddata.com/methodology/tags-data).

In 2025, [ACLED began including additional "conflict category" tags](https://acleddata.com/methodology/conflict-categories) on all events since 2020. These include Repression, Insurgency, Atrocities,Terrorist activity and Foreign military engagement. We'll try using the "Repression" tag to get a sense of what countries were using the most repression in some data from last year.

Note that we're pulling data for all countries, so we're going to pull data for a smaller time frame to ensure we can get a manageable amount of data. We'll also use the `event_types` option to remove all "Strategic developments", since these will never be tagged as repression events.

```{r}
#| eval: false

global_result<-acled_api(
  email = Sys.getenv('acled_email'),
  password = Sys.getenv('acled_password'),
  start_date = Sys.Date()-393,  # last year minus 4 more weeks
  end_date =Sys.Date()-365,     # last year
  population ='best',
  event_types = c('Battles', 
                  'Violence against civilians', 
                  'Protests', 
                  'Riots',
                  'Explosions/Remote violence'
                  )
  )

# saving the results to a file so we don't need to pull this again
write_csv(global_result, file='acled_global_events_October_2025.csv')


```



::: {.callout-tip title="Backup"}

If you're not able to get this working yet, you can download a copy of this data by running this code:

```{r}
global_result<-read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Neilblund/GVPT429KFall2026/refs/heads/master/Data/acled_global_events_October_2025.csv')


```

:::

Once we have our data, we'll do some additional filtering to identify repression events:

```{r}
repression<-global_result|>
  filter(str_detect(tags, "Repression"))

```

From here, we might do something like: aggregate the data to identify which countries had the highest number of repression related events during the time frame covered:

```{r}
repression|>
  group_by(country)|>
  summarize( n = n() )|> # getting the number of obs in each group
  arrange(-n)|>          # sorting in reverse order of frequency
  slice_head(n=10)       # getting the top 10

```

We could also visualize this using something like a bar plot:

```{r}
repression|>
  group_by(country)|>
  summarize( n = n() )|> 
  arrange(-n)|>          
  slice_head(n=10)|>
  ggplot(aes(y=reorder(country, n), # sorting the labels by n
             x=n)) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x= "Number of repression events",
       y = "Country",
       title ="Top 10 countries by number of repression events (October 2025)",
       caption = "Source: ACLED"
       ) 



```

# Interactive event mapping

We can use the leaflet package to create an interactive map of protest events in Hong Kong. Note that this kind of interactive plot only works with HTML formatted output, so you would need to use Rmarkdown to knit this as html before you could share it with someone else. That said, this can be a useful way to get a better grasp of your data even if you don't end up sharing it with anyone else.

```{r}
# install.packages("osmdata")
# install.packages("leaflet")
# install.packages('glue')

```

Start by creating a base mapping layer using the `addProviderTiles` function. This will just create an empty world map. You can try zooming in to look at specific areas here:

```{r}
library(leaflet)

base_map <- leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldStreetMap")  
base_map

```

We'll use the `getbb` function from the osmdata package to get the coordinates for Hong Kong. This will make it so our base map is automatically zoomed in to show the area of interest:

```{r}
hkbox  <- osmdata::getbb("Hong Kong, China")

event_map <- base_map |>
  fitBounds(
    lng1 = hkbox[1],
    lng2 = hkbox[3],
    lat1 = hkbox[2],
    lat2 = hkbox[4]
  )

event_map


```

Finally, we'll make some formatted pop-up markers that will show a bit more information about each event. The `glue` function here performs string interpolation, and the `<br>` tags are just HTML that creates a line break (this will be easier to understand once you take a look at the map)

For the sake of keeping things manageable, we'll only look at events that happened in 2019. I'll also remove events with low levels of geographic precision.

```{r}
hk_map_events <- hk_events|>
  filter(year(event_date) == 2019)|>
  filter(geo_precision == 1)|> # removing low-precision events
  mutate(formatted_notes = glue::glue('Date: {event_date}
                                      <br>
                                      Actor 1: {actor1}
                                      <br>
                                      Actor 2: {actor2}
                                      <br>
                                      Action: {sub_event_type}
                                      <br>
                                      Description: {notes}
                                      '))

```

Now we'll add markers for each event. Since many events happened in the same location, we'll use the `markerClusterOPtions` function to create a clustered marker that will spread out when we click or zoom in on a location:

```{r}
clustered_map <- event_map |>
  addAwesomeMarkers(
    data = hk_map_events,
    lng =  ~ longitude,
    lat =  ~ latitude,
    #icon = makeAwesomeIcon(icon = "Home", library = "glyphicon",
    #                       markerColor = 'red'
    #                       ), # uncomment to change the marker style 
    
    # groups together overlapping markers. Zoom in to show events
    clusterOptions = markerClusterOptions(),
    
    # create a popup to show additional info on reported events on click
    popup =  ~ formatted_notes
    
  )



clustered_map

```

You can also try swapping out the default basemap for something less "busy" using the [`addProviderTiles()`](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/basemaps.html) function. (Note that using some of these may require you to sign up for an account)

```{r}
clustered_map|>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.NatGeoWorldMap")




```
